issues.legal_issue: Rules governing essential incidents of mining leases apply to leases granted by auction when the auction chapter does not provide for those matters.
material_facts: The lease for extracting a minor mineral was granted by auction under the chapter governing auction and tender leases.
That chapter did not contain a corresponding rule governing the period of a mining lease.
issues.conclusion: The rules governing mining leases in the preceding chapter apply to auction leases so far as they address matters not provided for in the auction chapter, including the period of the lease.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1955, particularly Chapters IV and V. It reasoned that Chapter IV provisions governing essential incidents of a lease apply where Chapter V is silent, while rules that by their nature concern applications do not apply to auction grants. Rule 30 therefore applies to auction leases because the other applicable Chapter IV rules govern those leases and Chapter V has no corresponding rule. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.mining_lease_granted_by_auction: The government granted a mining lease through an auction process.
predicates.auction_rules_silent_on_lease_matter: The rules specifically governing auction leases did not provide for the matter at issue.

issues.definition: When a mining lease is granted by auction and the rules for auction leases do not address a matter, the rules governing that unprovided matter in the general lease chapter apply.

issues.legal_issue: The prescribed initial lease term and first extension cannot be shortened at the government’s discretion, and a further equivalent extension is available at the lessee’s option subject to the required investment guarantee.
material_facts: The lease was granted for a period shorter than five years through an auction, and the lessee accepted that period by bidding for and taking the lease.
The lessee sought an extension, but the government granted extensions totaling only eight months.
The lessee also sought renewal under the rule that provided for a further extension and an equivalent renewal option subject to an investment guarantee.
issues.conclusion: The shorter initial term was treated as having been desired by the lessee because the lessee accepted the lease on those terms. A first extension, if sought by the lessee, must be for five years; the lessee is entitled to an option for a further equivalent period if the required investment guarantee is given.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 30 of the Rajasthan Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1955, the word “may” in the main provision means “shall”: the initial term is five years unless the applicant desires a shorter term. In the proviso, “may” likewise means “shall” as to the first extension when the lessee desires it, and that extension must be five years. The proviso gives the lessee an option for a further equivalent period only on the required guarantee of investment in machinery, equipment, or the like. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: mining_lease_under_concession_rules and lessee_requests_first_extension and (not lessee_requests_further_extension or lessee_gives_required_investment_guarantee)

predicates.mining_lease_under_concession_rules: The lease is a mining lease governed by rules prescribing its term and extension arrangements.
predicates.lessee_requests_first_extension: The lessee asks to extend the lease beyond its initial term.
predicates.lessee_requests_further_extension: The lessee seeks the further extension available after the first extension.
predicates.lessee_gives_required_investment_guarant: The lessee guarantees the required investment in machinery, equipment, or similar items.

issues.definition: For a governed mining lease, the initial term is five years unless the lessee desires a shorter term, a requested first extension is five years, and a requested further equivalent extension is available if the lessee gives the required investment guarantee.

issues.legal_issue: A court may include a renewal option in its direction concerning a lease when that option is required by the governing rule, even if the relief sought does not expressly request the option.
material_facts: The lessee sought a direction for a five-year renewal under the governing rule but did not expressly ask for a further renewal option.
The rule required the first extension to include an option for a further equivalent period, subject to the prescribed guarantee.
The High Court directed an extension with that option, and the government argued that the direction exceeded the relief requested.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was competent to include the required renewal option in its direction; the direction accorded with the governing rule and did not grant improper relief beyond the prayer.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a request for renewal under Rule 30 is to be understood in light of the requirements of that rule, which makes the further renewal option a term of the first extension. It also held that, even if the prayer did not expressly include the option, the High Court could direct relief in accordance with the rule. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_challenges_writ_direction_on_leas: A party appeals against a writ court’s direction concerning the extension or renewal of a lease.
predicates.lessee_requests_renewal_under_governing_: The lessee asks for renewal under the rule governing the lease.
predicates.governing_rule_requires_option_as_term: The governing rule requires the relevant renewal option to form part of the lease extension.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a writ direction on a lease, the lessee has sought renewal under the governing rule, and that rule requires an option as part of the extension, the court may include that option in its direction.
